For mortgage qualification under Qualified Mortgage rules, total debt-to-income (including housing) must typically stay at or below 43%, though financial planners advise keeping overall debt payments well under that level [1].
Lenders may allow slightly higher ratios like 31%/43% only with documented justification and compensating factors [4].

response_text: Many sources define households as cost-burdened when monthly housing costs (including utilities, rent/mortgage, and related fees) exceed 30% of monthly income, with severe cost burden above 50% [2][4][8]. This 30% threshold aligns with HUD's standard for affordable housing and has been applied to over 40% of U.S. renter households in recent data [5][6]. For mortgage qualification under Qualified Mortgage rules, total debt-to-income ratios (including housing) generally should not exceed 43%, though lenders may justify higher ratios with compensating factors [1][3]. Financial planners typically advise keeping overall debt payments well below that 43% level [1]. DTI calculations divide all monthly debts by gross monthly income [7].

response_text: According to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, households are considered cost-burdened when spending more than 30% of income on rent, mortgage payments, and other housing costs, and severely cost-burdened above 50% [2][5][8]. For a standard Qualified Mortgage, monthly debt-to-income ratio (including the mortgage) generally must be at or below 43%, though planners recommend keeping it much lower [1]. The Bureau's updated QM rules replace the 43% DTI cap with a limit based on loan pricing [3]. FHA guidelines allow ratios of 31%/43% with justification for any excess [6]. Over 40% of U.S. renter households exceed the 30% housing cost threshold [7][9].

The standard benchmark is that housing costs (rent or mortgage plus utilities and fees) should not exceed 30% of monthly income to avoid being cost-burdened, per the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development definition used across multiple analyses [1][2][3][8][9]. Spending more than 50% is considered severely cost-burdened [1][2][9]. 

For qualified mortgages, total debt-to-income (including housing) is generally limited to 43%, though financial planners advise keeping overall debt payments far lower [4][5][6][7]. Over 19 million U.S. renter households exceeded the 30% threshold in recent data, with burdens concentrated in high-cost or low-income areas [3][8].

response_text: The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development defines households as cost-burdened when they spend more than 30% of income on housing costs such as rent, mortgage payments, utilities, and fees, with severe burden above 50% [3][4][5][6][8]. Over 40% of U.S. renter households exceed the 30% threshold [3][8]. For FHA loans, a front-end housing ratio of 31% is permissible (or 33% for certain energy-efficient loans), with the total debt-to-income ratio up to 43%; justification is required if either is exceeded [2]. General Qualified Mortgage standards also use a 43% total DTI limit based on loan pricing rather than a fixed ratio [1][9]. Financial planners recommend keeping all debt payments much lower than 43% of income [9].
